analysis.one_liner: Strips the consumer bureau's power to police "abusive" financial practices and hampers its enforcement.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have weakened the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's main enforcement tools against unfair and deceptive financial practices, was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on July 20, 2021 and never received a hearing or vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill removes the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's (CFPB) authority to take action against "abusive" acts and practices — the broadest of its three consumer-protection standards [S3]. It also bars the CFPB from acting against an unfair or deceptive practice until it has first consulted the company's primary financial regulator, and forces the bureau to follow the Federal Trade Commission's slower, more demanding process for writing rules [S3]. In effect, it makes it harder for the CFPB to sue companies that harm consumers and slower to write consumer-protection rules [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Financial companies that the CFPB can currently sue or fine for abusive practices — including lenders, debt collectors, credit-reporting firms, and other providers of consumer financial products — would face a lower legal bar and extra procedural hurdles before enforcement. Companies whose primary regulator is another agency would gain a consultation step that could delay CFPB action, and slower rulemaking means harmful practices could operate longer before rules catch up [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Lenders, debt collectors, and other CFPB-regulated firms

how_it_helps.text: Eliminates the CFPB's authority to take action against a person or service provider for an "abusive" act or practice, the broadest enforcement standard the bureau has under current law [S2].
Bars the CFPB from taking action against an unfair or deceptive act unless it first consults the company's primary financial regulatory agency, adding a step that can delay enforcement [S2].

Requires CFPB rulemaking on unfair or deceptive practices to comply with Federal Trade Commission rulemaking requirements, a process that historically has made consumer-protection rulewriting slower and more vulnerable to legal challenge [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary consumers. The "abusive" standard is one of the CFPB's main tools for going against practices like misleading loan terms, aggressive debt collection, and services that take unreasonable advantage of consumers; removing it narrows the cases the bureau can bring. Consultation requirements and slower rulemaking mean fewer enforcement actions and rules that arrive later, so consumers harmed by unfair practices would bear the cost [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers using loans, credit, and debt services

drawbacks.text: Defenders of the bill argue the FTC-style process and consultation with primary regulators would create more consistent rules across regulators and reduce duplicative or inconsistent enforcement against firms already supervised by another agency [S3].

However, the FTC's rulemaking requirements have historically made it difficult for regulators to issue broad consumer-protection rules, and eliminating the "abusive" standard removes the legal basis for many of the bureau's cases against practices that harm consumers without meeting the narrower definitions of "unfair" or "deceptive" [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits flow almost entirely to regulated financial companies in the form of lower legal exposure and slower rulemaking. The costs fall on consumers, who would lose the CFPB's broadest enforcement tool against practices that take unreasonable advantage of them. The bill's title frames it as uniformity and communication among regulators, but its concrete effect is to narrow and slow consumer enforcement [S2, S3].

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or vote, so it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Roger Williams of Texas and 11 Republican cosponsors introduced the bill in the House on July 20, 2021 [S1, S4].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, where no further action was ever taken on it [S5].
The bill never reached the House floor and was never considered in the Senate; it expired with the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers benefited from the bill's failure, because the CFPB kept its full authority to act against abusive, unfair, and deceptive financial practices. The financial firms the bill was written to shield from that authority did not get the relief they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers and the CFPB's enforcement powers

for.name: Rep. Roger Williams
for.role: Sponsor, House Financial Services Committee member

against.name: Rep. Maxine Waters
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee hearing or markup after its referral, leaving it to die in committee

sides.party_line_note: All 12 sponsors and cosponsors were House Republicans; the Democratic-controlled Financial Services Committee never acted on the bill.

industries.industry: Consumer finance firms (lenders, debt collectors, credit reporting, and other CFPB-regulated providers)
industries.note: The bill removes the "abusive" standard the CFPB uses to sue companies that take unreasonable advantage of consumers, and adds a required consultation with the firm's primary regulator before enforcement. That directly lowers these firms' legal exposure, and the cost shows up as consumers facing practices the bureau can no longer challenge.

Deposit-taking institutions supervised by other regulators would gain the most from the consultation requirement, which gives their primary regulator a chance to weigh in before the CFPB acts. Slower rulemaking also delays new consumer rules applying to their products.
Groups that rely on the CFPB's broad enforcement authority to challenge predatory practices would lose their strongest legal tool, since the bill strikes "abusive" from the bureau's mandate.
